stem: A hospital wants strong assurance its EHR recovery works but cannot risk any downtime of the live system. Which DR test is BEST suited?

options.text: A parallel test that runs recovery systems alongside live production
options.rationale: A parallel test validates that recovery actually works while production keeps running, giving high assurance without downtime.

options.text: A full-interruption test that shuts down production
options.rationale: A full-interruption test takes production down, which is unacceptable when downtime cannot be risked.
A checklist verifies plan completeness but does not prove recovery technically works.

options.text: No test, relying on the written plan
options.rationale: An untested plan provides no assurance that recovery will succeed.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders DR tests from least to most disruptive?

options.rationale: This is the standard escalation from least disruptive (checklist) to most disruptive (full-interruption).
This reverses the order; full-interruption is the most disruptive, not the least.
This ordering is scrambled and does not reflect increasing disruption.
This ordering is incorrect and mixes disruption levels arbitrarily.

stem: Which DR test provides the MOST realistic validation but also carries the greatest operational risk?

options.rationale: Failing fully over from shut-down production is the most realistic but riskiest test, since a failure can cause a real outage.
A checklist is the least disruptive and lowest-risk, not the most realistic.
A tabletop discussion does not touch systems, so it is neither the most realistic nor the riskiest.
A parallel test is realistic but keeps production up, carrying less risk than full-interruption.

stem: A team simply wants each member to individually review the DR plan to confirm it is complete and current, with no systems touched. Which test BEST describes this?

options.rationale: Individually reviewing the plan for completeness and currency, without touching systems, is the checklist test.
A full-interruption test shuts down production, far beyond a document review.
A parallel test runs recovery systems alongside production, not a mere document review.
A simulation role-plays a disaster scenario, more involved than an individual plan review.

stem: The recovery team gathers in a conference room and talks through a simulated disaster scenario step by step to verify roles and dependencies, without touching any systems. Which test is this?

options.rationale: Discussing a scenario together to validate roles and interdependencies without touching systems is a tabletop/walkthrough.
No systems are touched, so this is not a full-interruption test.
A parallel test actually runs recovery systems; the scenario describes only discussion.
A checklist is individual review; the scenario describes a group discussion of a scenario.

stem: An organization has never tested its DR plan and wants to build confidence responsibly. What is the BEST testing approach?

options.text: Progressive testing that starts with less disruptive tests and escalates as confidence grows
options.rationale: Building up through the levels catches plan gaps cheaply before undertaking high-risk tests.

options.text: Begin immediately with a full-interruption test for maximum realism
options.rationale: Jumping to the riskiest test on an untested plan can cause a real outage from unaddressed gaps.

options.text: Only ever perform checklist reviews and nothing more
options.rationale: Checklists alone never validate that recovery technically works.

options.text: Skip testing and update the plan annually on paper
options.rationale: Paper updates without testing leave the plan unproven.

stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes a parallel test from a full-interruption test?

options.text: A parallel test keeps production running while recovery runs alongside; a full-interruption test shuts production down and fails fully over
options.rationale: The key difference is production status: it stays up in a parallel test and goes down in a full-interruption test.
Only the full-interruption test shuts down production; the parallel test keeps it running.

options.text: A parallel test is riskier than a full-interruption test
options.rationale: The full-interruption test is riskier because it takes production offline.
Both actually run recovery systems; they are not document-only exercises.

stem: After completing a DR test that revealed several gaps, what is the MOST important follow-up action?

options.text: Document the findings and update the DR plan to close the gaps
options.rationale: Feeding test results back to update the plan is how testing improves recovery capability over time.

options.text: Discard the results since the test is over
options.rationale: Discarding findings wastes the test and leaves the gaps unaddressed.
Concealing gaps prevents remediation and undermines the plan.

options.text: Never test again to avoid finding more gaps
options.rationale: Avoiding testing leaves the plan unverified and gaps hidden, not fixed.

stem: What is the PRIMARY reason to test a disaster recovery plan?

options.text: To validate that recovery procedures work and objectives are achievable before a real disaster
options.rationale: Testing proves the plan actually functions, that RTO/RPO are achievable, and that staff know their roles.

options.text: To increase the plan's page count
options.rationale: Document length is not a purpose of testing.

options.text: To eliminate the need for backups
options.rationale: Testing does not remove the need for backups, which are part of what is tested.
Testing serves concrete validation goals, not idle curiosity.

stem: For a critical, always-on system that cannot afford unplanned downtime, which test is LEAST appropriate without careful authorization and mitigations?

options.rationale: Shutting down an always-on critical system risks a real outage if the test fails, making it least appropriate without strong safeguards.
A checklist touches no systems and poses essentially no operational risk.
A discussion-based walkthrough poses no risk to production.
A parallel test keeps production running and is relatively low risk.

stem: Ranking by disruption, which DR test sits between a simulation and a full-interruption test?

options.rationale: In the escalation order, the parallel test is more disruptive than a simulation but less than a full-interruption test.
The checklist is the least disruptive, at the bottom of the order, not between simulation and full-interruption.
The tabletop is near the bottom of the order, below simulation.
Full-interruption is the most disruptive endpoint, not a step between others.

stem: What is the PRIMARY characteristic of a parallel test?

options.text: Recovery systems process real workloads alongside production, which remains operational
options.rationale: A parallel test runs recovery in parallel with a still-running production environment to validate recovery without downtime.

options.text: Production is completely shut down during the test
options.rationale: That describes a full-interruption test; production stays up in a parallel test.

options.text: No systems are used, only a discussion occurs
options.rationale: That describes a tabletop; a parallel test actually runs recovery systems.

options.text: Only individual document review is performed
options.rationale: That describes a checklist test, not a parallel test.

stem: A company must prove to a regulator that failover completely works, and it has an authorized maintenance window in which brief downtime is acceptable. Which test provides the highest-confidence proof?

options.text: A full-interruption test conducted during the authorized window
options.rationale: When downtime is authorized and acceptable, a full-interruption test offers the most realistic, highest-confidence proof that failover works.
A checklist cannot prove failover technically works, so it is insufficient for the regulator's requirement.
A discussion validates understanding but does not demonstrate actual failover.

options.text: No test, citing the maintenance window as proof
options.rationale: Having a window is not proof; an actual test must be performed.

stem: A manager claims that passing a checklist review proves the organization can recover from a disaster. Why is this reasoning MOST flawed?

options.text: A checklist only confirms the plan is complete and current; it does not demonstrate that recovery technically works
options.rationale: Document review validates plan currency but never exercises actual recovery, which requires parallel or full-interruption testing.

options.text: A checklist shuts down production, which is dangerous
options.rationale: A checklist touches no systems and does not shut down production.

options.text: A checklist is more disruptive than a full-interruption test
options.rationale: A checklist is the least disruptive test, not the most.

options.text: A checklist requires failing over to the alternate site
options.rationale: A checklist involves no failover; it is a document review.

stem: A team role-plays a realistic disaster scenario, exercising some support functions and decision-making, but stops short of failing over production. Which test BEST describes this?

options.rationale: A simulation role-plays a disaster and may exercise support functions while stopping short of a production failover.
The scenario explicitly stops short of failing over production, so it is not full-interruption.
A checklist is a passive document review, not an active role-played scenario.
A parallel test actually runs recovery systems on real workloads; the scenario stops short of failover.

stem: Which approach to DR testing is LEAST advisable for an organization that has never exercised its plan?

options.text: Immediately performing a full-interruption test on critical production systems
options.rationale: Starting with the riskiest test on an untested plan invites a real outage from undiscovered gaps; escalation should be gradual.
Beginning with the least disruptive test is sound, low-risk practice.

options.text: Following a checklist with a tabletop exercise
options.rationale: Escalating gradually to a tabletop is appropriate progressive testing.
A parallel test after lower-level tests is a reasonable next step, not the least advisable.

stem: A DR plan references servers and staff that no longer exist after a reorganization. Which testing benefit would BEST have caught this?

options.text: Testing verifies plan currency, revealing that the plan no longer matches the environment
options.rationale: Even a low-level review test surfaces stale references, ensuring the plan reflects the current environment.

options.text: Testing increases the number of backups automatically
options.rationale: Testing validates the plan; it does not automatically create backups.
Encryption is unrelated to detecting stale plan content.

options.text: Testing eliminates the need to maintain the plan
options.rationale: Testing complements maintenance; it does not remove the need to keep the plan updated.

stem: Which DR test is the LEAST disruptive to normal operations?

options.rationale: An individual document review touches no systems and is the least disruptive test.
A full-interruption test shuts down production and is the most disruptive.
A parallel test runs recovery systems and is more disruptive than a checklist.
A simulation role-plays a scenario and is more involved than a checklist review.

stem: A team needs to actually confirm recovery works technically, but any production outage is unacceptable. Which single test BEST balances high assurance with zero production downtime?

options.rationale: A parallel test exercises real recovery alongside running production, delivering strong assurance with no production downtime.
It would cause the unacceptable production outage the constraint forbids.
A checklist gives low assurance and does not confirm recovery technically works.
A tabletop validates understanding but does not technically confirm recovery.

stem: How does DR testing PRIMARILY connect to the ongoing improvement of the recovery capability?

options.text: Test findings feed back into updating the plan, forming a continuous improvement cycle
options.rationale: Documented test results drive plan updates and maintenance, keeping recovery capability effective over time.

options.text: Testing is a one-time event with no follow-up
options.rationale: Testing should be recurring, with findings feeding continuous improvement.

options.text: Testing replaces the need for a plan
options.rationale: Testing validates and improves the plan; it does not replace it.

options.text: Testing only matters for compliance paperwork
options.rationale: Testing provides real operational assurance and improvement, not just paperwork.
